orientation.summary: This is the 2025 update to Hawai'i's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), produced by the Hawai'i Department of Land and Natural Resources (DLNR). It covers the full range of native wildlife in Hawai'i—over 1,400 Species of Greatest Conservation Need spanning terrestrial, freshwater, anchialine, and marine taxa. The document treats climate change as a major threat category (named explicitly alongside invasive species and habitat loss) and discusses observed and projected climate impacts extensively, including coral bleaching, upslope mosquito expansion, sea-level rise, drought, and wildfire. Discussion of range shifts per se is limited: the document mainly frames climate impacts as range expansions of mosquitoes and diseases into previously disease-free high-elevation forest bird refugia (an upslope shift of a biotic stressor), and shrinkage of suitable habitat for native species. Most analyses are narrative syntheses drawing on published science; the plan does not itself run SDMs, vulnerability models, or connectivity models but references vulnerability assessments as an information gap and describes a new Maui Nui Landscape Conservation Plan being developed to spatially prioritize conservation actions.

Hawai'i is more prone to wildfire due to climate change, which is causing temperatures to increase and rainfall to decrease.

Climate change models of rainfall for the Hawaiian Islands through the remainder of the century predict, on average, a decrease in rainfall and reduced availability of freshwater resources (Timm et al. 2015), particularly in the dry climatic regions.

Current research efforts focus on two main approaches to determine the potential impacts of climate change on individual species: estimating species vulnerabilities and projecting responses of species to expected changes. Vulnerability assessments are essentially syntheses of available information that are used to determine the potential impacts of a threat (e.g., climate change) on species of interest. Typically, vulnerability assessments attempt to determine species' vulnerability by estimating species' exposure to climate change, their sensitivity to such changes, and their adaptive capacity to respond to change.

evidence_index.text: Forest birds in Hawai'i face an uncertain future as the effects of climate change exacerbate existing threats caused by disease and the steady loss of habitat. Increases in mean temperature, declining precipitation, and changes in stream flow associated with climate change appear to be allowing the upward spread of mosquitos and increased transmission of avian malaria to highly susceptible native forest birds.
evidence_index.location: Species Vulnerability Assessments in Response to Changing Climate

evidence_index.text: Temperature increases will allow avian disease pathogens and vectors to expand their ranges to higher elevations, and will increasingly dry out wet forest habitat upon which kāhuli tree snails, picture-wing Drosophila and other invertebrates depend. Consequently, the small areas that currently support the last remaining populations of many rare native species will continue to shrink.

sea level rise (SLR) will inundate the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (NWHI), reducing habitat for nesting seabirds, native passerines, monk seals, and sea turtles, and altering coastal habitats throughout Hawai'i.

Increases in seawater temperature also contributes to the phenomenon of coral bleaching, in which corals temporarily or permanently expel their symbiotic algae, potentially resulting in the death of the corals.

Among the higher-elevation MHI, a significant portion of native plants are threatened by future climate conditions, owing to shifts or even complete losses of climatic niches of some species (Fortini et al. 2013). Some native plant communities may be able to expand up to higher elevation ranges as temperatures warm, but those at the highest elevations may have no place to go.

Increasing temperatures, moving up slope, will greatly expand the higher-elevation viability and thus range of mosquitoes and the diseases they transmit (Benning et al. 2002, Atkinson and LaPointe 2009, Atkinson et al. 2014). This trend underscores the need to protect high elevation refugia for susceptible native birds

Some populations of the 'amakihi have developed infection survival mechanisms to malaria and now are found again in lowland habitats (Foster et al. 2007, Eggert et al. 2008, Atkinson et al. 2013, Neddermeyer et al. 2023), indicating disease resistance may evolve. This potential further emphasizes the need to protect, restore, and manage an elevational range of forests
Predicted drying conditions from climate change will increase the length and severity of drought and increase the risk of future wildland fire, affecting wildlife populations.

Chronic drought conditions on Maunakea have contributed to the recent decline of the endangered palila and other native birds (Banko et al. 2013). Palila survival and reproduction are closely tied to the species' primary shelter and food source, māmane (Sophora chrysophylla).

evidence.text: In 2011 and 2012 a total of 50 Nihoa millerbirds were translocated from Nihoa Island to Laysan Island...The initial population of 50 birds has increased to more than 400 birds.

Between 1999 and 2012, 222 captive-bred puaiohi were released into the wild on Kaua'i. Initially, the program was successful, with several captive-raised birds documented successfully breeding, but in later releases, survival and recruitment was lower.
ʻAkiapōlāʻau however have responded extremely well to koa reforestation, and populations at Hakalau forest have increased by more than 900% in the koa planting areas.

evidence_of_efficacy.absence_note: The document contains numerous references to ongoing management actions and some case studies with outcome data (particularly for bird translocations and habitat restoration). However, evidence specifically tied to climate adaptation actions (e.g., translocations motivated by climate change) is presented at a general level. Score = 2 for limited but present evidence from prior projects with documented outcomes.
projects: Nihoa millerbird translocation (2011-2012): 50 birds translocated from Nihoa to Laysan Island; population grew to >400 birds, demonstrating translocation efficacy for island passerines.

Puaiohi captive release program (1999-2012): 222 captive-bred birds released on Kauai; initial success with breeding documented, but later releases showed lower survival; program discontinued based on monitoring results — provides evidence of both partial efficacy and limitations.

Koa reforestation at Hakalau Forest NWR: 'Akiapola'au populations increased by >900% in koa planting areas, providing strong field evidence that habitat restoration supports native forest bird recovery.
